paras: If you have ever worked on a contract between a Brazilian company and an American one, you have probably noticed that the two legal teams do not think in the same way. It is not only a question of language. Most of the world's legal systems belong to one of two great traditions, common law and civil law, and each of them has trained its lawyers to ask a different first question.

The common law was born in England after the Norman Conquest of 1066, when royal judges began to travel around the country deciding disputes. Because there was no single written code, what the judges relied on was their own earlier decisions. Over the centuries, this practice became a principle known as precedent: a court is expected to follow what higher courts have already decided in similar cases. It is often said that common law is made by judges, and to some extent this is true. Faced with a new problem, an American or English lawyer will usually look for a case first.

The civil law tradition, which is followed in Brazil, France, Germany and most of Latin America, has its roots in Roman law. Its modern form owes a great deal to the French Civil Code of 1804, written under Napoleon, which was copied or adapted across Europe and far beyond it. In this tradition, the starting point is the code itself: a written, organized body of rules approved by the legislature. A Brazilian lawyer facing the same problem would probably open the Civil Code before reading any judgment. The judge's role, at least in theory, is to apply the law, not to create it.

In practice, however, the two traditions have been moving closer for decades. Common law countries now have enormous bodies of written statutes, and in Brazil, certain decisions of the Federal Supreme Court have been binding on lower courts since a constitutional reform in 2004. Had the two systems stayed as far apart as they were two centuries ago, international contracts would be much harder to negotiate today. For a lawyer who works across borders, the lesson is clear: the important thing is not to decide which tradition is better, but to understand which question the other side is going to ask first.

listenings.text: Today I want to look at one Latin phrase that sits at the center of the common law: stare decisis. It means, more or less, to stand by things decided. When a higher court has decided a legal question, lower courts are expected to decide the same question in the same way. Why does this matter so much? Mainly because of predictability. If similar cases are decided in similar ways, people and companies can plan. A business that signs a contract can predict how a court is likely to read it. But precedent is not a prison. A court can depart from its own earlier decisions, although it does so rarely and with care. The most famous example in the United States is Brown versus Board of Education, in 1954. In that case, the Supreme Court rejected the idea of separate but equal, which it had accepted in Plessy versus Ferguson almost sixty years earlier. So the system is stable, but it is not frozen.

When I applied for my master's degree in the United States, I had to take the TOEFL, and my first practice test was a disaster. I read the first passage the way I read a contract: every word, slowly, twice. By the third passage, I had run out of time. A friend who had taken the test told me to change my method completely. Now I skim the passage first, and I read the first sentence of each paragraph with special care, because that is usually where the main idea is. Then I go to the questions, and I scan the text for the answer to each one. With multiple choice, I try to rule out the wrong options before I choose the right one. The trick is that the correct answer is almost never verbatim. It is a paraphrase of the text. The wrong options often use the exact words of the passage, and that is what makes them dangerous.

extra_audio.text: First, Pedro skims the whole passage to get the general idea. Then he reads the topic sentence of each paragraph with special care. Next, he reads the first question and scans the text for the answer. After that, he rules out the options that cannot be right. Finally, he chooses the option that paraphrases the text, not the one that repeats it word for word.
